claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Auditory fear conditioned mice significantly increased their freezing behavior during the tone conditioned stimulus (CS) presentation.
claims.source: As expected, the auditory fear conditioned mice significantly increased their freezing behavior during the tone conditioned stimulus (CS) presentation (Figure 1E, repeated-measures ANOVA, F(35,210) = 11.303, p<0.001), particularly during tone-on periods compared to tone-off periods (Figure 1F left, paired samples t-test, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Control mice that did not undergo auditory fear conditioning showed virtually no freezing during the tone presentation.
claims.source: In contrast, control mice that did not undergo auditory fear conditioning showed virtually no freezing during the tone presentation (Figure 1E and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The mean of all normalized pyramidal neuronal activities recorded in the aIC remained steady during the experiment in both groups.
claims.source: The mean of all normalized (z-scored) pyramidal neuronal activities recorded in the aIC remained steady during the experiment in both groups (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The conditioned group showed no significant correlation between the normalized firing rate and freezing behavior.
claims.source: The conditioned group showed no significant correlation between the normalized firing rate and freezing behavior, nor was there any difference in the mean firing rate between the tone-on and tone-off periods (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: There was no difference in the mean firing rate between the tone-on and tone-off periods in the conditioned group.
claims.source: The conditioned group showed no significant correlation between the normalized firing rate and freezing behavior, nor was there any difference in the mean firing rate between the tone-on and tone-off periods (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The power of aIC local field potential in the <50 Hz frequency tended to be reduced in the conditioned group compared to the control during CS.
claims.source: Similarly, the power of aIC local field potential in the <50 Hz frequency, which includes the theta frequency, tended to be reduced in the conditioned group compared to the control during CS (Figure 1I and J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by local field potential data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Theta frequency (6 Hz) was significantly reduced during, but not before, CS presentation in the conditioned group compared to the control.
claims.source: Quantitative analysis revealed that theta frequency (6 Hz) was significantly reduced during, but not before, CS presentation in the conditioned group compared to the control (Figure 1K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by local field potential data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Among the neurons recorded from fear conditioned mice, 29.6% were responsive and 70.4% were non-responsive.
claims.source: Among the neurons recorded from fear conditioned mice, 29.6% were responsive (n=32/108) and 70.4% were non-responsive (n=76/108; Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Among the responsive cells, there were proportionally more freezing-excite cells (65.6%) than freezing-inhibited cells (34.4%).
claims.source: Among the responsive cells, there were proportionally more freezing-excite cells (n=21/32, 65.6%) than freezing-inhibited cells (n=11/32, 34.4%), but the trend was not statistically significant (binomial proportions test, p=0.11; Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The trend of more freezing-excited cells than freezing-inhibited cells was not statistically significant.
claims.source: Among the responsive cells, there were proportionally more freezing-excite cells (n=21/32, 65.6%) than freezing-inhibited cells (n=11/32, 34.4%), but the trend was not statistically significant (binomial proportions test, p=0.11; Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Freezing-excited cells tended to be recorded in the middle and deep layers (L5 and 6).
claims.source: The freezing-excited cells tended to be recorded in the middle and deep layers (L5 and 6; Figure 2C, red dots), while the freezing-inhibited cells tended to be recorded in the superficial and middle layers (L2/3, 4, and 5; Figure 2C, blue dots).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of recording locations presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Freezing-inhibited cells tended to be recorded in the superficial and middle layers (L2/3, 4, and 5).
claims.source: The freezing-excited cells tended to be recorded in the middle and deep layers (L5 and 6; Figure 2C, red dots), while the freezing-inhibited cells tended to be recorded in the superficial and middle layers (L2/3, 4, and 5; Figure 2C, blue dots).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of recording locations presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Freezing-inhibited cells showed relatively higher tone-off firing rates, which decreased during tone presentation.
claims.source: Freezing-inhibited cells showed relatively higher tone-off firing rates, which decreased during tone presentation (Figure 2D, conditioned upper).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Freezing-excited cells showed a lower tone-off firing rate that increased during tone presentation.
claims.source: Freezing-excited cells, in contrast, showed a lower tone-off firing rate that increased during tone presentation (Figure 2D, conditioned lower).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Non-responsive cells showed an intermediate tone-off firing rate between those of the freezing-inhibited and freezing-excited cells and remained relatively constant throughout the recording.
claims.source: The non-responsive cells, interestingly, showed an intermediate tone-off firing rate between those of the freezing-inhibited and freezing-excited cells and remained relatively constant throughout the recording (Figure 2D, conditioned middle).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The activities of the freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neurons were significantly correlated with freezing behavior in opposite directions.
claims.source: Pearson's correlation coefficient between mean normalized firing rate and freezing of each neuronal response type revealed that the activities of the freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neurons were significantly correlated with freezing behavior in opposite directions (Figure 2F; freezing-excited cell r=0.81, p<0.05; freezing-inhibited cell r=–0.68, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: No correlation was found between non-responsive neurons and freezing behavior.
claims.source: As expected, no correlation was found for the non-responsive neurons (r=0.13, p=0.44).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The tone-induced firing rate peaks of the freezing-inhibited and freezing-excited cells were significantly different.
claims.source: The tone-induced firing rate peaks of the freezing-inhibited and freezing-excited cells were significantly different (Figure 2G, Mann-Whitney U Test, p<0.05); the freezing-inhibited cells peaked at 10.5 s, while the freezing-excited cells peaked at 17.6 s.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by temporal analysis of neuronal recording data and statistical testing presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The freezing-inhibited cells peaked at 10.5 s.
claims.source: The tone-induced firing rate peaks of the freezing-inhibited and freezing-excited cells were significantly different (Figure 2G, Mann-Whitney U Test, p<0.05); the freezing-inhibited cells peaked at 10.5 s, while the freezing-excited cells peaked at 17.6 s.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by temporal analysis of neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The freezing-excited cells peaked at 17.6 s.
claims.source: The tone-induced firing rate peaks of the freezing-inhibited and freezing-excited cells were significantly different (Figure 2G, Mann-Whitney U Test, p<0.05); the freezing-inhibited cells peaked at 10.5 s, while the freezing-excited cells peaked at 17.6 s.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by temporal analysis of neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: None of the recorded aIC neurons were tone-onset or tone-offset cells.
claims.source: However, none of the recorded aIC neurons, neither the conditioned group's nor the control's, were tone-onset or tone-offset cells (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: None of the neuronal activity of control mice significantly correlated with the tone.
claims.source: None of the neuronal activity of control mice (n=14 cells, 3 mice) significantly correlated with the tone (r=0.027, p=0.87), but a subset of aIC neurons in conditioned mice showed significant correlation with tone (freezing-excited cells, r=0.44, p<0.05, n=9; freezing-inhibited cells, r=−0.51, p<0.05, n=5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: A subset of aIC neurons in conditioned mice showed significant correlation with tone.
claims.source: None of the neuronal activity of control mice (n=14 cells, 3 mice) significantly correlated with the tone (r=0.027, p=0.87), but a subset of aIC neurons in conditioned mice showed significant correlation with tone (freezing-excited cells, r=0.44, p<0.05, n=9; freezing-inhibited cells, r=−0.51, p<0.05, n=5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: None of the recorded cells correlated with tone during fear extinction.
claims.source: Interestingly, none of the recorded cells correlated with tone (Figure 2M).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of neuronal recording data during fear extinction presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited cells found in the aIC of fear-conditioned mice are highly correlated with freezing behavior, not tone.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that the freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited cells found in the aIC of fear-conditioned mice are highly correlated with freezing behavior, not tone.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation analyses comparing neuronal activity with freezing behavior and tone during fear expression and extinction.

claims.claim: Neither activation of ChR2 nor NpHR3 triggered any aberrant behaviors in the open-field test.
claims.source: Neither activation of ChR2 nor NpHR3 triggered any aberrant behaviors, and locomotion did not differ among groups (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the open-field test presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Locomotion did not differ among groups in the open-field test with optogenetic stimulation.
claims.source: Neither activation of ChR2 nor NpHR3 triggered any aberrant behaviors, and locomotion did not differ among groups (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the open-field test presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: ChR2 stimulation increased brain rhythms in the 20 Hz and 40 Hz range.
claims.source: ChR2 stimulation increased brain rhythms in the 20 Hz and 40 Hz range (Figure 3D, spectrogram) because light stimulation was delivered at 20 Hz pulses.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by local field potential data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Continuous light for NpHR3 stimulation did not induce specific frequency modulation.
claims.source: Continuous light was delivered for NpHR3 stimulation, so it did not induce specific frequency modulation (Figure 3E, spectrogram).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by local field potential data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Optostimulation of the aIC neurons did not induce aberrant seizure-like synchronized activities.
claims.source: Simultaneous local field potential (LFP) and single unit analysis before, during, and after optical stimulations confirmed that optostimulation of the aIC neurons did not induce aberrant seizure-like synchronized activities.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simultaneous LFP and single unit recording data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: During a 30 s tone +optostimulation, there was no difference in freezing behavior among groups.
claims.source: During a 30 s tone +optostimulation, there was no difference in freezing behavior among groups (Figure 3G; Kruskal-Wallis, H(2) = 2.489, p=0.288).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: During the tone-off sessions, freezing behavior among groups differed significantly.
claims.source: However, during the tone-off sessions, freezing behavior among groups differed significantly (Figure 3G; Kruskal-Wallis, H(2) = 22.937, p=0.000; post hoc Mann-Whitney, ChR2 vs. control p=0.000; NpHR vs. control p=0.019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Conditioned freezing responses of the ChR2 group were sustained even after tone +optostimulation ended, and tended to accumulate with repeated stimulations, particularly during the tone-off sessions.
claims.source: Conditioned freezing responses of the ChR2 group were sustained even after tone +optostimulation ended, and tended to accumulate with repeated stimulations, particularly during the tone-off sessions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: In the NpHR3 group, freezing immediately decreased after tone +optostimulation ended.
claims.source: In the NpHR3 group, freezing immediately decreased after tone +optostimulation ended (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Inhibition of aIC pyramidal neurons (NpHR3) reduced the freezing level between the first and the last tone +optostimulation.
claims.source: When comparing the freezing behavior of each group during their first and last tone +optostimulation trials, inhibition of aIC pyramidal neurons (NpHR3) reduced the freezing level between the first and the last tone +optostimulation (Figure 3H, left; Wilcoxon signed test, p=0.063).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: During the tone-off period, the ChR2 group significantly increased freezing after the last stimulation compared to the first.
claims.source: During the tone-off period, the ChR2 group significantly increased freezing after the last stimulation compared to the first (Figure 3H, right; Wilcoxon signed test, **p<0.01).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Group differences in fear expression were absent in the experiment carried out without optostimulation.
claims.source: These group differences in fear expression were absent in the experiment carried out without optostimulation (ANOVA group effect: F(2,30) = 1.076, p=0.354; Figure 3I and J), confirming that group differences in fear expression were induced by the activation or inhibition of pyramidal neurons in the aIC.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Group differences in fear expression were induced by the activation or inhibition of pyramidal neurons in the aIC.
claims.source: These group differences in fear expression were absent in the experiment carried out without optostimulation (ANOVA group effect: F(2,30) = 1.076, p=0.354; Figure 3I and J), confirming that group differences in fear expression were induced by the activation or inhibition of pyramidal neurons in the aIC.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of behavioral results with and without optostimulation.

claims.claim: None of the neurons in the aIC expressed both green and red fluorophores.
claims.source: Surprisingly, none of the neurons in the aIC expressed both green and red fluorophores, suggesting that non-overlapping populations of aIC neurons project to the medial dorsal thalamus and the amygdala (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The aIC neurons projecting to the medial dorsal thalamus appeared mainly in the deep layers (approximately layer 6).
claims.source: The neurons projecting to the medial dorsal thalamus and the amygdala were also located in different layers within the aIC; the aIC neurons projecting to the medial dorsal thalamus appeared mainly in the deep layers (approximately layer 6), while the aIC neurons projecting to the amygdala appeared in a relatively more superficial layer (approximately layer 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of retrograde tracing data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The aIC neurons projecting to the amygdala appeared in a relatively more superficial layer (approximately layer 5).
claims.source: The neurons projecting to the medial dorsal thalamus and the amygdala were also located in different layers within the aIC; the aIC neurons projecting to the medial dorsal thalamus appeared mainly in the deep layers (approximately layer 6), while the aIC neurons projecting to the amygdala appeared in a relatively more superficial layer (approximately layer 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of retrograde tracing data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The number of aIC neurons projecting to the medial dorsal thalamus was greater than those projecting to the amygdala.
claims.source: The number of aIC neurons projecting to the medial dorsal thalamus was greater than those projecting to the amygdala even though they were populated in a more restricted area (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of retrograde tracing data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The aIC→medial thalamus neurons could be freezing-excited cells.
claims.source: Collectively, data suggest that the aIC→medial thalamus neurons could be freezing-excited cells, while the aIC→amygdala neurons may be freezing-inhibited cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculated based on the comparison of recording locations and tracing results.

claims.claim: The aIC→amygdala neurons may be freezing-inhibited cells.
claims.source: Collectively, data suggest that the aIC→medial thalamus neurons could be freezing-excited cells, while the aIC→amygdala neurons may be freezing-inhibited cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculated based on the comparison of recording locations and tracing results.

claims.claim: The aIC projection to the thalamus terminated mainly in the MD and CM regions.
claims.source: As shown in the sample expression patterns, the aIC projection to the thalamus terminated mainly in the MD and CM regions (Figure 5B), while the aIC projection to the amygdala terminated mainly in the BLA and CeA (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of viral expression patterns presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The aIC projection to the amygdala terminated mainly in the BLA and CeA.
claims.source: As shown in the sample expression patterns, the aIC projection to the thalamus terminated mainly in the MD and CM regions (Figure 5B), while the aIC projection to the amygdala terminated mainly in the BLA and CeA (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of viral expression patterns presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Activating the aIC→medial thalamus projection significantly reduced freezing compared to the control.
claims.source: While activating the aIC→medial thalamus projection significantly reduced freezing compared to the control (Figure 5C, blue line; repeated measures ANOVA, F(1, 17)=10.666, *** p<0.001), activating the aIC→amygdala projection significantly enhanced freezing compared to the control (Figure 5G, red line; repeated measures ANOVA, F(1, 12)=23.663, *** p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic manipulation data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Activating the aIC→amygdala projection significantly enhanced freezing compared to the control.
claims.source: While activating the aIC→medial thalamus projection significantly reduced freezing compared to the control (Figure 5C, blue line; repeated measures ANOVA, F(1, 17)=10.666, *** p<0.001), activating the aIC→amygdala projection significantly enhanced freezing compared to the control (Figure 5G, red line; repeated measures ANOVA, F(1, 12)=23.663, *** p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic manipulation data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: When opto-stimulation was turned off, and only the conditioned tone was delivered (retrieval test), there were no differences in the freezing level between groups.
claims.source: Also, when opto-stimulation was turned off, and only the conditioned tone was delivered (retrieval test), there were no differences in the freezing level between groups (Figure 5C and G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the retrieval test presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Activation of neither the aIC→medial thalamus nor the aIC→amygdala projection produced any lasting behavioral effects between light stimulations.
claims.source: In addition, we compared freezing levels of tone +optostim and tone-off periods to assess whether activation of these pathways produces a lasting effect on behavior. Unlike the phenomenon observed in aIC activation with ChR2 (Figure 3F), activation of neither the aIC→medial thalamus nor the aIC→amygdala projection produced any lasting behavioral effects between light stimulations (Figure 5D and H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data comparing tone+optostim and tone-off periods presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: In the pIC, a significantly larger population of excitatory neurons was reported compared to inhibitory neurons.
claims.source: In the pIC, a significantly larger population of excitatory neurons was reported compared to inhibitory neurons (Casanova et al., 2018), but in the aIC, we found approximately equal number of freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claims.claim: In the aIC, approximately equal number of freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neurons were found.
claims.source: In the pIC, a significantly larger population of excitatory neurons was reported compared to inhibitory neurons (Casanova et al., 2018), but in the aIC, we found approximately equal number of freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: An E/I imbalance has been linked to various disorders, such as epilepsy, schizophrenia, and autism spectrum disorder.
claims.source: An E/I imbalance has been linked to various disorders, such as epilepsy, schizophrenia, and autism spectrum disorder (Yizhar et al., 2011).

results.result: Fear-conditioned mice showed significantly increased freezing during tone presentation compared to controls, while the mean normalized firing rate of all aIC pyramidal neurons remained steady in both groups. Theta frequency power was significantly reduced during CS presentation in conditioned mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C34 are well-supported by behavioral and electrophysiological data with appropriate statistical tests (repeated-measures ANOVA, paired t-tests, Mann-Whitney U tests). The findings demonstrate successful fear conditioning and provide baseline characterization of population-level aIC activity. Sample sizes (11 conditioned mice, 3 control mice) appear adequate for behavioral measures, though control group is small.

results.result: Single-unit recordings revealed that 29.6% of aIC pyramidal neurons were responsive to freezing behavior, with freezing-excited cells (65.6%) and freezing-inhibited cells (34.4%) showing opposite correlations with freezing. These cell types differed in their baseline firing rates, laminar locations, and temporal dynamics during CS presentation.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C48 are supported by comprehensive single-unit recording data with appropriate correlation analyses and statistical tests. The classification of neurons based on Pearson correlation (p<0.05) is methodologically sound. The temporal analysis showing different peak times (10.5s vs 17.6s) for freezing-inhibited vs freezing-excited cells is particularly compelling. However, the non-significant trend (p=0.11) for more freezing-excited than freezing-inhibited cells (C37) should be interpreted cautiously.

results.result: During fear expression, a subset of aIC neurons in conditioned mice showed significant correlation with tone, but during fear extinction, no neurons correlated with tone. This suggests that freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited cells are highly correlated with freezing behavior rather than tone per se.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 are supported by correlation analyses during both fear expression and extinction paradigms. The extinction experiment (Figure 2I-M) provides critical evidence distinguishing tone-related from freezing-related activity. The logic is sound: if neurons correlated with freezing during expression but not with tone during extinction (when freezing decreases), they likely encode freezing rather than tone. However, the sample size for extinction (N=7 mice, 35 cells) is relatively small.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation parameters (ChR2 at 20Hz, NpHR3 continuous) did not induce aberrant behaviors, affect locomotion, or produce seizure-like activity, as confirmed by open-field testing and simultaneous LFP/single-unit recordings.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 provide essential control data demonstrating that optogenetic manipulations are specific and do not produce confounding effects. The open-field test, LFP analysis, and single-unit recordings during stimulation provide converging evidence. These controls are critical for interpreting subsequent behavioral experiments. Sample sizes appear adequate (ChR2 n=13, NpHR3 n=7, Control n=13).

results.result: Optogenetic manipulation of aIC pyramidal neurons bidirectionally modulated fear behavior, with excitation (ChR2) increasing freezing and inhibition (NpHR3) decreasing freezing, particularly during tone-off periods. These effects were absent without optostimulation, confirming specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C65 are well-supported by optogenetic behavioral data with appropriate statistical tests (Kruskal-Wallis, Wilcoxon signed test, ANOVA). The finding that effects were most pronounced during tone-off periods (C59) is interesting but complicates interpretation. The control experiment without optostimulation (C64-C65) is essential and strengthens the conclusion. However, the marginal significance for NpHR3 effect (p=0.063, C62) should be noted.

results.result: Retrograde tracing revealed that non-overlapping populations of aIC neurons project to the medial dorsal thalamus (mainly layer 6) versus the amygdala (mainly layer 5), with more neurons projecting to the thalamus than to the amygdala.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by dual retrograde tracing experiments with clear histological evidence (Figure 4). The finding of non-overlapping populations (no double-labeled neurons) is striking and well-documented. The laminar segregation and quantification of projection neurons are appropriately analyzed. Sample size (N=3 mice) is modest but typical for anatomical tracing studies.

results.result: Based on the laminar distribution of recorded neurons and projection patterns, the authors speculate that aIC→medial thalamus neurons could be freezing-excited cells while aIC→amygdala neurons may be freezing-inhibited cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 are explicitly speculative (using 'could be' and 'may be') and lack direct evidence linking single-unit recordings to projection targets. While the laminar distributions are suggestive, this remains a hypothesis requiring direct testing (e.g., combining retrograde tracing with electrophysiology or calcium imaging). The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation in the Discussion.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of aIC→medial thalamus projections significantly reduced freezing, while activation of aIC→amygdala projections significantly enhanced freezing. These effects were specific to stimulation periods and did not persist during retrieval tests or between stimulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C77 are strongly supported by pathway-specific optogenetic experiments with robust statistical evidence (repeated measures ANOVA, p<0.001 for both pathways). The bidirectional modulation is clear and compelling. The control experiments showing no effect during retrieval (C76) and no lasting effects between stimulations (C77) strengthen the interpretation. Sample sizes are adequate (aIC→thalamus: ChR2 n=12, control n=8; aIC→amygdala: ChR2 n=6, control n=6).

results.result: General aIC activation produced residual behavioral effects during inter-trial periods when optostimulation was off, which was not due to seizure activity but may result from recruitment of multiple brain areas, as specific pathway activation did not produce lasting effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99 describe an interesting phenomenon with adequate supporting evidence. The absence of seizure activity is well-documented (C97, supported by LFP and single-unit data). The speculation about mechanism (C98-C99) is reasonable given the comparison between general aIC activation and specific pathway activation. However, the exact mechanism remains unclear and would benefit from additional investigation.

results.result: The aIC regulates conditioned fear through bidirectional control at multiple levels: balanced freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neuronal activity at the local circuit level, and distinct populations projecting to different brain regions (amygdala increasing fear, medial thalamus decreasing fear).
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C8 and C113-C115 represent the main conclusions of the study, integrating findings from single-unit recordings, optogenetics, and neural tracing. The evidence is comprehensive and internally consistent across multiple experimental approaches. The bidirectional modulation is demonstrated at both the cellular level (freezing-excited vs freezing-inhibited neurons) and circuit level (aIC→amygdala vs aIC→medial thalamus). Statistical support is robust throughout.

results.result: The aIC shows approximately equal numbers of freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neurons (unlike pIC which has more excitatory neurons), suggesting the aIC maintains E/I balance at the cellular level. Temporal differences in their activity may create windows for signal gating while maintaining global E/I balance.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C86 integrate the current findings with prior literature to propose a mechanistic framework. The comparison with pIC (C78, citing Casanova et al., 2018) is appropriate. The E/I balance concept is well-established (C80, C84). However, claims C83, C85, and C86 are partially speculative, as the study did not directly measure group-level activity changes or test the signal gating hypothesis. The reasoning is sound but requires further experimental validation.

results.result: The aIC may be specialized for regulating subjective fear and integrating anxiety and fear information, potentially receiving differential inputs from prefrontal cortex (to freezing-inhibited cells) and amygdala (to freezing-excited cells).
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C92 are largely speculative, drawing on prior literature (Nicolas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2022; Gehrlach et al., 2020) and human studies to propose functional specialization. While the integration with existing literature is appropriate, these claims represent hypotheses rather than demonstrated findings. The proposed input patterns (C91-C92) are inferred from connectivity studies but not directly tested here.

results.result: This study demonstrates for the first time that controlling distinct aIC outputs bidirectionally regulates fear behaviors, suggesting that merely controlling total aIC output may be sufficient for therapeutic effects without specifically targeting freezing-excited or freezing-inhibited cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 and C104 represent important translational implications supported by the optogenetic data showing bidirectional modulation. The novelty claim (C104) appears justified as this is the first demonstration of pathway-specific bidirectional fear modulation from aIC. However, the therapeutic implications (C93-C94) are speculative extrapolations from mouse data and should be interpreted cautiously. The logic is sound but clinical validation would be required.

results.result: The findings are consistent with prior studies showing amygdala activation promotes fear while thalamus activation reduces fear. The extensive connectivity of the insular cortex suggests multiple redundant circuits may fine-tune fear behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C108 appropriately contextualize the findings within existing literature. The consistency with prior work (C100-C101, citing Johansen et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2011; Baek et al., 2019) strengthens the interpretation. The acknowledgment of potential antidromic activation (C102-C103) is important for methodological transparency. The speculation about redundant circuits (C108) is reasonable given the known connectivity (C107, citing Gehrlach et al., 2020) but remains hypothetical.

results.result: The study used only male mice (F1 hybrids of C57BL/6J×129S4/SvJaeJ, 10-18 weeks old). While many studies report no sex differences in cued fear conditioning, the underlying circuit mechanisms may differ between sexes, and the bidirectional fear modulation observed here may be different in females.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 and C120 appropriately acknowledge a significant limitation of the study. The use of only male mice is clearly stated (C120), and the authors appropriately discuss potential sex differences (C109-C112, citing Day and Stevenson, 2020). The distinction between behavioral similarity and circuit similarity (C110) is an important conceptual point. This limitation should be addressed in future studies.

results.result: The introduction establishes that the aIC is implicated in fear regulation in humans and animals, has distinct anatomical connections from pIC, and is ideally positioned to integrate high-level information, though how aIC connections to different brain regions modulate fear remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C24 provide appropriate background from prior literature with proper citations. These claims establish the rationale for the study by reviewing human imaging studies (C1-C2, C11-C13), animal studies (C14-C16), and anatomical organization (C17-C24). The knowledge claims are well-supported by the cited literature and provide clear motivation for investigating aIC circuit mechanisms in fear conditioning.

results.result: The study analyzed 108 putative pyramidal neurons (93% of isolated neurons) from 11 mice, distinguished from 8 putative interneurons (7%) based on action potential characteristics.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 describe the neuronal sample analyzed in the study. The classification method (action potential characteristics) is standard and appropriate. The proportions (93% pyramidal, 7% interneurons) are consistent with expected cortical composition. The sample size of 108 pyramidal neurons from 11 mice is adequate for single-unit analysis, though the control group (14 neurons from 3 mice) is relatively small.

results.result: The findings contribute to understanding neural circuits underlying fear behavior and have potential implications for developing therapeutic strategies for fear and anxiety disorders. All experiments were conducted with appropriate ethical approval and in accordance with ARRIVE 2.0 guidelines.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C119 provide appropriate concluding statements and methodological transparency. The contribution to understanding fear circuits (C116) is well-supported by the data. The therapeutic implications (C117) are appropriately framed as potential rather than demonstrated. The ethical statements (C118-C119) provide necessary documentation of proper conduct and reporting standards.

results.result: Single-unit recordings in the aIC revealed balanced populations of freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited pyramidal neurons (approximately equal numbers, though not statistically significant), with distinct laminar distributions (freezing-excited in deep layers L5-6, freezing-inhibited in superficial/middle layers L2/3-5), temporal dynamics (different peak times), and strong correlations with freezing behavior but not tone presentation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding, stating 'the activity contrast between the units that increase/decrease firing during freezing is clear' and noting 'roughly equal populations that increased or decreased firing during freezing.' The characterization of neural activity is treated as convincing evidence for bidirectional control.

results.result: Optogenetic manipulation of aIC pyramidal neurons bidirectionally modulated conditioned freezing: ChR2 activation increased freezing (particularly during tone-off periods with cumulative effects), while NpHR3 inhibition reduced freezing, with effects confirmed to be specific to optogenetic manipulation and not due to seizure activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the paper as providing 'convincing data on the role of anterior insular circuits in bidirectionally controlling fear' using 'optogenetic control of neural activity.' The bidirectional modulation is explicitly acknowledged as a strength demonstrating behavioral control.

results.result: Neural tracing revealed non-overlapping populations of aIC neurons projecting to the medial thalamus versus amygdala, with distinct laminar distributions (medial thalamus projections in deep layer 6, amygdala projections in more superficial layer 5) and greater numbers of thalamus-projecting neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the anatomical findings, noting 'the anterior insular cortex contains non-overlapping neurons which project to the mediodorsal thalamus or amygdala' with distinct laminar clustering patterns. This anatomical segregation is treated as established fact in the review.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of anatomically defined aIC output pathways bidirectionally modulated fear: aIC→medial thalamus activation decreased freezing while aIC→amygdala activation increased freezing, with effects specific to stimulation periods and no lasting effects between trials, demonstrating for the first time that distinct aIC outputs regulate fear behaviors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state 'Stimulation of insula-thalamus projection decreased freezing behavior, and stimulation of insula-amygdala projections increased fear behavior,' affirming the bidirectional control via anatomically defined outputs. This is recognized as demonstrating 'bidirectional control of behavior, linking the underlying anatomy and physiology.'

results.result: Based on the overlap between recording locations and projection patterns, the authors infer that aIC→medial thalamus neurons could be freezing-excited cells while aIC→amygdala neurons may be freezing-inhibited cells, which would provide a mechanism to reduce overexpression of fear.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly identify this as a weakness, stating 'The link between spiking, anatomy, and behavior requires assumptions/inferences: the anatomically/genetically defined neurons which had distinct outputs and opposite behavioral effects can only be assumed the increased/decreased spiking neurons, based on the rough area of cortical layer they were recorded.' The authors acknowledge this limitation ('we do not have a direct link'), and reviewers note 'This is, of course, discussed as a future experiment.'

results.result: Fear-conditioned mice showed significantly increased freezing during tone presentation compared to controls, while mean aIC neuronal activity remained steady and showed no overall correlation with freezing or tone, though theta frequency power was reduced during CS presentation in conditioned mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question the basic behavioral paradigm or population-level neural activity measurements. The behavioral effects are implicitly accepted as the foundation for subsequent analyses of single-unit responses.

results.result: Single-unit recordings yielded 108 putative pyramidal neurons (93% of isolated neurons) distinguished from 8 putative interneurons (7%) based on action potential characteristics.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praise the use of extracellular spiking activity, noting 'It is nice to see the recording of extracellular spiking activity, which provides a clear measure of neural output, whereas similar studies often use bulk calcium imaging.' The cell-type classification is not questioned.

results.result: The residual behavioral effects of general aIC activation (but not specific pathway activation) may occur due to recruitment of multiple brain areas or recurrent circuits modulated by aIC neurons, particularly given aIC connections with motor-related regions.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic speculation about residual effects is not directly addressed by reviewers. While they acknowledge the phenomenon, they do not evaluate the proposed explanations, leaving this interpretation uncertain.

results.result: Human studies have implicated the aIC in subjective fear regulation and anxiety disorders, with increased IC activity during fear conditioning in healthy subjects and even greater activity in anxiety disorder patients.
results.evaluation: These background claims from human literature are not questioned by reviewers and serve as accepted motivation for the study. Reviewers focus on the novel rodent findings rather than challenging the human literature context.

results.result: The authors propose that the aIC maintains excitation/inhibition balance at the cellular level through temporal differences in freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited cell activity, potentially creating windows for signal processing, and suggest that merely controlling total aIC output may be sufficient for therapeutic regulation of fear without needing to target specific cell types.
results.evaluation: These interpretive and speculative claims about E/I balance mechanisms and therapeutic implications are not directly evaluated by reviewers. While the underlying data on balanced populations is supported, the mechanistic and clinical interpretations represent author speculation that reviewers neither affirm nor challenge.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on behavioral and population-level electrophysiology claims (C28-C34). Both evaluations support the fear conditioning paradigm and baseline aIC activity characterization. OpenEval notes small control group size, while peer reviewers implicitly accept these foundational measurements.

Perfect agreement on neuronal classification claims (C25-C27). Both support the cell-type identification methodology. Peer reviewers explicitly praise the use of extracellular spiking activity, while OpenEval notes adequate sample size with relatively small control group.

Strong agreement on single-unit recording data (C35-C48). Both support the classification of freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neurons. Peer reviewers describe the activity contrast as 'clear,' while OpenEval notes the non-significant trend (p=0.11) for population differences should be interpreted cautiously. Both evaluations treat this as convincing evidence for bidirectional control.

Agreement on extinction experiment claims (C49-C52). Both support the logic distinguishing tone-related from freezing-related activity. OpenEval notes relatively small sample size (N=7 mice, 35 cells), while peer reviewers incorporate this into their broader affirmation of bidirectional neural populations.

Strong agreement on anatomical tracing claims (C66-C69). Both affirm the non-overlapping projection populations and laminar segregation. Peer reviewers treat this as established fact, while OpenEval notes the modest but typical sample size (N=3 mice) for anatomical studies.

Agreement on optogenetic control validation claims (C53-C57). Both support the specificity controls. Peer reviewers emphasize this as 'convincing data' for bidirectional control, while OpenEval highlights the importance of these controls for interpreting subsequent behavioral experiments.

Agreement on general optogenetic behavioral modulation claims (C58-C65). Both support the bidirectional effects. OpenEval notes the marginal significance for NpHR3 (p=0.063) and interesting tone-off effects, while peer reviewers focus on the overall demonstration of behavioral control.

Strong agreement on pathway-specific optogenetic claims (C72-C77). Both affirm the bidirectional modulation via anatomically defined outputs with robust statistical evidence. Peer reviewers explicitly state the opposite behavioral effects of insula-thalamus vs insula-amygdala stimulation, while OpenEval emphasizes the robust statistics (p<0.001) and control experiments.

Agreement on uncertainty regarding linking single-unit recordings to projection targets (C70-C71). Both identify this as speculative. Peer reviewers explicitly call this a weakness requiring 'assumptions/inferences,' noting the authors acknowledge lacking 'a direct link.' OpenEval similarly marks this as 'UNCERTAIN' and notes it requires direct testing.

Partial overlap on seizure-related claims (C95, C97). OpenEval supports the absence of seizure activity and finds the mechanistic speculation reasonable. Peer reviewers acknowledge the phenomenon but do not directly evaluate the proposed explanations in R8.

Both address mechanistic speculation about residual effects (C98-C99). OpenEval finds the speculation reasonable given the comparison between general and pathway-specific activation. Peer reviewers do not directly evaluate these mechanistic explanations, leaving interpretation uncertain.

Partial agreement on main conclusions (C3). Both support the bidirectional control finding. Peer reviewers affirm 'roughly equal populations that increased or decreased firing during freezing,' while OpenEval integrates this with comprehensive evidence across multiple experimental approaches.

Partial agreement on main conclusions (C4). Both support the optogenetic bidirectional modulation. Peer reviewers describe 'convincing data' on bidirectional control, while OpenEval emphasizes the integration of findings across cellular and circuit levels.

Partial agreement on main conclusions (C5). Both support the anatomical segregation finding. Peer reviewers affirm non-overlapping projection neurons, while OpenEval integrates this with the broader circuit-level findings.

Strong agreement on main conclusions about pathway-specific effects (C6-C8). Both support the bidirectional control via anatomically defined outputs. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm opposite behavioral effects of the two pathways, while OpenEval emphasizes robust statistical support throughout.

Partial overlap on E/I balance concepts (C79). OpenEval supports the integration with prior literature on E/I balance but notes some claims are speculative. Peer reviewers affirm the underlying balanced populations but do not directly evaluate the mechanistic interpretations in R10.

Divergent evaluations on mechanistic speculation (C83, C85, C86). OpenEval marks these as 'SUPPORTED' while noting partial speculation about group-level activity and signal gating. Peer reviewers mark these as 'UNCERTAIN,' neither affirming nor challenging the mechanistic interpretations.

Divergent evaluations on therapeutic implications (C93-C94). OpenEval marks as 'SUPPORTED' while noting these are speculative extrapolations requiring clinical validation. Peer reviewers mark as 'UNCERTAIN,' not directly evaluating these clinical interpretations.

Agreement on novelty claim (C104). Both support this as the first demonstration of pathway-specific bidirectional fear modulation from aIC. Peer reviewers incorporate this into their affirmation of the bidirectional control findings.

Agreement on background literature claims (C1-C2, C11-C13). Both support these as appropriate motivation from human imaging studies. Peer reviewers do not question these background claims, while OpenEval affirms they are well-supported by cited literature.

Partial overlap on human literature context (C89). OpenEval marks speculative claims about functional specialization as 'UNCERTAIN,' while peer reviewers accept human literature context without challenge but do not evaluate the specific interpretations.

Divergent evaluations on speculative mechanistic claims (C90). OpenEval marks as 'UNCERTAIN' noting these are hypotheses drawing on prior literature. Peer reviewers also mark as 'UNCERTAIN,' neither affirming nor challenging the speculation.

Partial overlap on limitations (C105). OpenEval supports the contextualization with existing literature and acknowledgment of potential antidromic activation. Peer reviewers incorporate this into their discussion of the link between anatomy and physiology requiring assumptions.

OpenEval addresses sex differences limitation (C109-C112, C120), appropriately noting the use of only male mice and potential sex differences. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific limitation.

OpenEval supports concluding statements and methodological transparency (C116-C119), including therapeutic implications and ethical statements. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these concluding claims.
